# Tidewater fleet maintenance manual

This manual is the engineering department's reference for keeping the
Tidewater fleet in class. It covers the two route vessels, MV Kestrel and
MV Osprey, and the relief vessel MV Heron, which Tidewater charters from
Dunmere Marine Services every winter while one of the route vessels is out
of service. Where a rule differs between vessels, the vessel is named; where
it doesn't, the rule applies to all three.

## Dry-dock schedule

Every vessel in the fleet is taken out of the water at regular intervals so
that the hull below the waterline, the propellers, the rudders, the sea
chests and the anodes can be inspected and repaired. The classification
society sets the longest interval it will accept; Tidewater's own intervals
are shorter, because the Harlow estuary is shallow and silty and the vessels
touch bottom more often than a typical coastal ferry. Dry-docking is always
planned for the quiet months between November and February, and never for
two route vessels in the same winter, so that the timetable can run with one
route vessel and the relief vessel.

The yard is Pellin Slipway for anything under 45 metres and the Dunmere
graving dock for anything longer. A dry-dock period normally takes between
nine and fourteen days, including the tow or passage to the yard, and the
chief engineer signs the vessel back into service only after a sea trial
with full astern and a crash-stop test.

MV Osprey, the smaller foot-passenger vessel, is dry-docked every 24 months.
Its aluminium hull is inspected for galvanic corrosion around the water-jet
intakes at each visit, and its anodes are replaced whatever their condition.
MV Heron is the charterer's responsibility and is dry-docked by Dunmere
Marine Services every 36 months; Tidewater only checks the certificate
before accepting the vessel for the winter. MV Kestrel, the vehicle ferry,
is dry-docked every 30 months, and at every second visit its bow thruster
tunnel is shot-blasted and recoated, which adds about four days to the
period.

## Hull and propeller inspections between dry-docks

Between dry-docks, a diver inspects each route vessel's hull, propellers and
rudders. The inspection is filmed and the recording is kept with the vessel's
maintenance record for six years. The diver is contracted from Harlow
Commercial Diving and must hold a current surface-supplied diving
certificate; Tidewater crew never dive on the vessels themselves.

A diver inspection is also required after any grounding, after any contact
with a floating object that the master reports, and after any vibration that
the engine room cannot explain within one watch. In those cases the vessel
may continue in service only with the chief engineer's written agreement,
and at a reduced service speed of 10 knots until the diver has reported.

The routine diver inspection happens every 6 months for MV Kestrel and every
4 months for MV Osprey, whose water-jet intakes collect debris faster. Any
blade damage deeper than 3 millimetres on a propeller, or any intake grille
that has lost more than one bar, takes the vessel out of service until it
has been repaired.

## Lifesaving equipment

The lifesaving equipment on every vessel is inspected weekly by the bosun
and annually by an approved service station. The weekly inspection covers
the liferafts' hydrostatic releases, the rescue boat's engine (run for five
minutes), the lifebuoys and their lights, the immersion suits for the crew,
and the lifejacket lockers. Any item found missing or damaged is logged in
the defect system before the next sailing, and the vessel may not sail if
the total lifejacket count falls below what the rules below require.

Adult lifejackets are carried for every passenger the vessel is certified to
carry, plus the crew. Child lifejackets are carried for at least 10% of the
passenger certificate on MV Kestrel. On MV Osprey, which carries more school
groups, the rule is stricter: 20% of the passenger certificate in child
lifejackets, plus 12 infant lifejackets kept in the locker by the forward
boarding door. Spare adult lifejackets are carried on both vessels at 5% of
the passenger certificate, rounded up, and are stowed separately from the
main lockers so that they are not counted twice during the weekly check.

## Engine overhauls

MV Kestrel has two medium-speed diesel engines driving controllable-pitch
propellers. Each engine is overhauled on running hours, not on the
calendar: a top overhaul (cylinder heads, injectors, valves) every 12,000
running hours and a major overhaul (pistons, liners, bearings) every 24,000
running hours. The two engines are never overhauled in the same month.

MV Osprey has four high-speed diesel engines driving two water jets. Its
engines are exchanged rather than overhauled on board: an engine that
reaches 15,000 running hours is removed and replaced with a reconditioned
unit from the manufacturer, and the removed engine is returned for
reconditioning. The exchange takes one working day per engine and is done
at the Harlow berth overnight.

## Fuel policy

Fuel is bunkered at Harlow only. The Pellin Island and Dunmere berths have
no bunkering facilities, and a vessel must therefore always carry enough fuel
to return to Harlow even if it cannot berth at the far end of the route and
has to hold off the island in bad weather.

The master checks the fuel quantity before every departure from Harlow and
records it in the deck log. The minimum reserve depends on the route. For a
Pellin Island crossing, a vessel must leave Harlow with at least 25% of its
fuel capacity on board. For a Dunmere crossing, which is longer and more
exposed, the minimum is 40% of capacity, and the master may not waive it.
When the forecast includes winds above 30 knots, both minimums rise by a
further 10 percentage points.

## Defect reporting

Every defect is logged in the defect system with a photograph, the location
on the vessel and the name of whoever found it. The chief engineer assigns
each defect a category: category A defects affect safety and must be fixed
before the next sailing; category B defects must be fixed within 7 days;
category C defects are fixed at the next planned maintenance period. A
category B defect that is still open after 7 days becomes category A
automatically, and the operations manager is notified by the defect system.
